answer_1.quote: Through several experiments on captioning datasets such as MS-COCO, Flickr8k, we find that CLAIR correlates surprisingly well with human preferences, outperforming prior captioning measures.

answer_2.quote: We benchmark against several existing measure of caption similarity. BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR and CIDEr all primarily measure ngram overlap (however have different weighting schemes between n-grams, and across precision/recall). We also compare against SPICE, which compares caption parse trees and focuses on matching perceived action and object relationships in addition to n-grams. While the aforementioned measures are commonly reported in image captioning works, we also compare against several modern measures, including CLIP-Score which uses the recent CLIP model for reference-free evaluation.

answer_3.quote: We introduce CLAIR (Criterion using LAnguage models for Image caption Rating), a measure which scores a candidate caption based on the likelihood that it describes the same image as a set of references by directly asking an LLM to produce a numeric rating.

answer_4.quote: we run several evaluations that compare scores generated by CLAIR to both human judgments of caption quality and other image captioning evaluation measures.
answer_4.guideline: humans were presented with two candidate caption sets (two image captioning models, OFA and BLIP using different temperatures), and asked which candidate caption set correlated better with a reference caption set on two measures: how much they overlapped factually (correctness), and how much information they provided about the references (coverage).
